us_senate.note: No U.S. Senate seat is up in California in 2026. Alex Padilla's term runs through January 2029 (Class 3, next election 2028) and Adam Schiff's through January 2031 (Class 1, next election 2030).

incumbent.name: Gavin Newsom
incumbent.note: Term-limited; ineligible to run. Endorsed Becerra after the primary.

candidates.name: Xavier Becerra
candidates.bio: Former U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services (2021-2025), California Attorney General (2017-2021) and 12-term U.S. Representative from Los Angeles (1993-2017).
candidates.platform: Becerra campaigns under the slogan 'Build, Protect, and Lead California,' listing health care, housing, affordability, energy and utility costs, homelessness, wildfire and disaster preparedness, and artificial intelligence as priorities. He calls himself a 'Health Care Governor,' proposing near-term cost containment while working toward a universal single-payer CalCare system, and a 'Power Hour' program to reduce utility bills. He also emphasizes his record of litigation against the Trump administration as Attorney General.

candidates.name: Steve Hilton
candidates.bio: London-born political commentator and former Fox News host (2017-2023) who was director of strategy to U.K. Prime Minister David Cameron, co-founded Crowdpac and the policy group Golden Together, and has not previously held elected office.
candidates.platform: Hilton's message is 'Great jobs, great homes, great kids' and ending what he calls one-party Democratic rule. His 'Califordable' agenda targets $3.00 gasoline by repealing certain fuel rules and fees, halving utility bills, exempting the first $150,000 of income from state income tax, and cutting fees and red tape to build starter homes. His 'CaliFuture' agenda calls for every student reading by third grade, skills training in every school, shrinking the state bureaucracy and abolishing the $800 minimum small-business tax.

offices.likely_winner_basis: Every public general-election poll since June shows Becerra ahead by 10-30 points, and all major forecasters rate the race Solid/Safe Democratic.
offices.summary: Democrat Xavier Becerra, former U.S. HHS Secretary and California Attorney General, faces Republican commentator Steve Hilton to succeed term-limited Gov. Gavin Newsom. Becerra finished first in a 61-candidate June primary (27.98%) with Hilton second (24.59%), while fellow Democrat Tom Steyer (22.79%) and Republican Chad Bianco (10.17%) were eliminated. The two debated once on CNN on Sept. 30, 2026; Republicans have not won a California governor's race since 2006.

incumbent.name: Eleni Kounalakis
incumbent.note: Term-limited; running for State Treasurer instead.

candidates.name: Fiona Ma
candidates.bio: Certified public accountant serving as California State Treasurer since 2019, previously a San Francisco Supervisor (2002-2006), Assemblymember (2006-2012) and Board of Equalization member (2015-2019).
candidates.platform: Ma's voter-guide statement says too many Californians are being priced out and stresses using her financial background to focus on affordability, accountability, transparency, cutting waste and reducing red tape for housing and small businesses. She cites her Treasurer record on financing affordable housing and down-payment assistance, and says as Lieutenant Governor she will work to make higher education more affordable, expand paid internships and strengthen career pathways.

candidates.name: Gloria Romero
candidates.bio: Former Democratic state Senate Majority Leader (2005-2008) who served in the Assembly (1998-2001) and Senate (2001-2010), authored the 2010 'parent trigger' school law, and joined the Republican Party in 2024.
candidates.platform: Romero's voter-guide statement says one-party rule has failed on homelessness, cost of living, schools and public safety; she pledges to restore education standards, develop an economic plan for businesses, rein in what she calls politicized commissions affecting water and farmland, defend Title IX in girls' sports and fight campus antisemitism. In interviews she has emphasized phonics-based reading, teacher tenure reform, standardized testing in UC admissions and using the Lieutenant Governor's seats on state boards and the State Lands Commission to address housing costs and regulation.

offices.likely_winner_basis: Ma led the June primary and the Independent Voter Project's September survey projects her at about 57% in a two-way race; the office has been held by Democrats since 2011.
offices.summary: State Treasurer Fiona Ma (D) and former state Senate Democratic majority leader Gloria Romero, now a Republican, advanced from a crowded 18-candidate primary in which Ma took 19.12% and Romero 17.83%; Democrats Josh Fryday (14.73%) and Michael Tubbs (13.27%) were eliminated. Incumbent Eleni Kounalakis is term-limited and is running for Treasurer. The race has drawn little polling; the California Democratic Party endorsed Ma after the primary.

incumbent.name: Rob Bonta
incumbent.note: Running for re-election to a second full term.

candidates.name: Rob Bonta
candidates.bio: Incumbent Attorney General, appointed by Gov. Newsom in April 2021 and elected to a full term in 2022, after serving in the State Assembly (2012-2021) and on the Alameda City Council; the first Filipino American to hold the office.
candidates.platform: Bonta frames his re-election around protecting freedoms, defending democracy and standing up to what he calls unlawful federal power grabs, citing roughly 100 lawsuits against the Trump administration. His issues page lists stopping gun violence, fighting hate crimes and protecting civil rights, targeting transnational criminal organizations, protecting health care and reproductive freedom, consumer and worker protection, environmental enforcement and standing up for immigrant communities.

candidates.name: Michael Gates
candidates.bio: Huntington Beach attorney who served as elected city attorney of Huntington Beach from 2014 to 2025 and in 2025 as a Deputy Assistant Attorney General in the Civil Rights Division of the U.S. Department of Justice.
candidates.platform: Gates's voter-guide statement says California ranks sixth nationally in violent crime and pledges to fully enforce Proposition 36 against repeat theft and drug offenses, prosecute fentanyl traffickers, protect victims and move homeless people into treatment. His campaign site lists public safety ('Making Crime Illegal Again'), fully funding police and defending officers in court, local control against Sacramento, government accountability, Title IX and parental rights, enforcing camping and loitering laws, and election integrity.

offices.likely_winner_basis: Bonta won an outright majority (56.62%) in the June primary against the same opponent and Sabato's Crystal Ball rates the seat Safe Democratic; no public general-election poll was found.
offices.summary: Incumbent Democrat Rob Bonta seeks a second full term against Republican Michael Gates, the former Huntington Beach city attorney. Bonta took 56.62% in the three-candidate primary to Gates's 37.94%, with Green Marjorie Mikels (5.44%) eliminated. Bonta has emphasized litigation against the Trump administration, while Gates has centered his campaign on crime and public safety.

incumbent.name: Shirley Weber
incumbent.note: Running for re-election to a second full term.

candidates.name: Shirley Weber
candidates.bio: Incumbent Secretary of State, appointed in January 2021 and elected to a full term in 2022, previously a State Assemblymember (2012-2021) and longtime San Diego State University professor who helped found its Africana Studies department.
candidates.platform: Weber says her central commitment is protecting and expanding voting rights, pledging that 'nothing stands between you and the ballot box' and citing her defense of California's election laws in court. Her campaign lists working with county election officials to expand ballot access, improving transparency of election, lobbyist and campaign-finance filings, upgrading the office's cybersecurity, and expanding voter registration among students, rural residents and formerly incarcerated Californians. She has said she prioritizes accuracy over speed in vote counting.

candidates.name: Donald P. Wagner
candidates.bio: Orange County Supervisor for District 3 since 2019 (board chairman 2023-2025), former Mayor of Irvine (2016-2019), former State Assemblymember (2010-2016) and business attorney.
candidates.platform: Wagner says he is running to make elections 'secure, efficient, accurate, and accessible' and to ensure only eligible voters cast ballots, pledging to speed up vote counting, clean up voter rolls and support the Proposition 39 voter-ID initiative. He describes the Secretary of State as a nonpartisan 'umpire for fair elections' and also calls for making the office's business-filings division more small-business friendly.

offices.likely_winner_basis: Weber won 58.70% outright in the June primary, and Sabato's Crystal Ball rates the office Safe Democratic.
offices.summary: Incumbent Democrat Shirley Weber, first elected in 2022 with 60.1%, faces Republican Orange County Supervisor and former Assemblymember Don Wagner. Weber took 58.70% in the primary to Wagner's 36.74%; two Green Party candidates were eliminated. Weber has campaigned on defending voting access and election administration, while Wagner has emphasized voter-roll maintenance and election integrity.

incumbent.name: Fiona Ma
incumbent.note: Term-limited; running for Lieutenant Governor instead.

candidates.name: Eleni Kounalakis
candidates.bio: Lieutenant Governor since 2019, former U.S. Ambassador to Hungary (2010-2013) and former president of the Sacramento housing developer AKT Development; she left the 2026 governor's race in August 2025 to run for Treasurer.
candidates.platform: Kounalakis says she will 'responsibly manage California's finances, strengthen our economy, and make smart investments,' with stated goals of using public finance to build more affordable housing, investing in children and families, defending health care and immigrant communities, and protecting pensions. She cites her background as a builder and her Lieutenant Governor record on the State Lands Commission, UC Regents and CSU Trustees.

candidates.name: Jennifer Hawks
candidates.bio: Retired Palo Alto businesswoman and former school administrator.
candidates.platform: Hawks presents herself as 'not a career politician' and pledges to bring transparency and accountability to the Treasurer's office, exposing waste, fraud and mismanagement and publishing where state money goes. Her site lists day-one initiatives including publishing office findings, reviewing state investment holdings, creating a unified public debt dashboard and scrutinizing housing-finance spending. She also cites bringing bond debt under control and protecting retirement security through the Treasurer's seats on the CalPERS and CalSTRS boards.

offices.likely_winner_basis: Kounalakis, a two-term statewide officeholder, led the primary by nearly 13 points over a first-time Republican candidate in a state Democrats have swept statewide since 2010; no public poll found.
offices.summary: Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis (D), who left the governor's race in August 2025 to run for Treasurer, faces Republican Jennifer Hawks, a retired businesswoman. Kounalakis led the six-candidate primary with 36.69%; Hawks edged Democratic state Sen. Anna Caballero (16.40%) and Republican David Serpa (12.87%) for second with 24.00%. Incumbent Fiona Ma is term-limited and running for Lieutenant Governor.

incumbent.name: Malia Cohen
incumbent.note: Running for re-election to a second term.

candidates.name: Malia Cohen
candidates.bio: Incumbent State Controller since January 2023, previously a member of the State Board of Equalization (2019-2023) and the San Francisco Board of Supervisors (2011-2019).
candidates.platform: Cohen says she is seeking re-election to manage taxpayer dollars 'with transparency, accountability, and fairness,' citing expanded public access to financial and payroll data, timely monthly cash reports, unclaimed-property returns and modernization of the state payroll system. News coverage describes her platform as modernizing FI$Cal and stabilizing state payroll, increasing audits and transparency, and urging budget caution. Her site lists broader priorities including housing, retirement security, health care, reproductive access and climate.

candidates.name: Herb Morgan
candidates.bio: San Diego-area financial advisor with about four decades in finance who founded an investment firm later acquired by Cantor Fitzgerald, served as Cantor Fitzgerald's Chief Investment Officer (2017-2026), and formerly sat on the San Diego City Employees' Retirement System board.
candidates.platform: Morgan's campaign centers on 'radical transparency': placing all state expenditures in a public online database with transaction-level, near-real-time detail, which he says he can build under existing Controller authority. He pledges to audit government spending including a full audit of social services, expose waste and fraud (citing EDD and health care), use AI-driven tools and blockchain-backed ledgers to modernize oversight, and meet federal audit and financial-reporting deadlines.

offices.likely_winner_basis: Cohen won an outright majority (56.80%) in the primary against the same opponent; the 2022 Controller race was the closest statewide contest (55.35%-44.65%) but still a double-digit Democratic win. No public poll found.
offices.summary: Incumbent Democrat Malia Cohen seeks a second term against Republican Herb Morgan, a San Diego-area financial executive and former San Diego City Employees' Retirement System board member. Cohen took 56.80% in the three-way primary to Morgan's 37.53%, with Peace and Freedom candidate Meghann Adams (5.67%) eliminated. The Controller is the state's chief fiscal officer and sits ex officio on the Board of Equalization.

candidates.name: Jane Kim
candidates.bio: Civil rights attorney who served on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors (District 6, 2011-2019) and later as California director of the Working Families Party; ballot designation Attorney/Consumer Advocate.
candidates.platform: Kim's campaign centers on lowering costs, guaranteed coverage and fast and fair claims. She proposes a publicly run 'Disaster Insurance for All' program, capping what she calls excessive insurer profits and CEO pay, cracking down on price-fixing, and requiring insurers to pay interest when they delay, deny or underpay valid claims. She pledges to refuse contributions from insurance companies, fossil fuel companies and corporate PACs.

candidates.name: Ben Allen
candidates.bio: Democratic state senator for District 24 (in the Senate since 2014) whose district includes the Pacific Palisades area burned in the January 2025 fires.
candidates.platform: Allen says he is running to reform the insurance system, lower costs and protect consumers, and does not accept insurance-industry contributions. He proposes increasing competition to bring insurers back to California, holding insurers accountable for denied or delayed claims, improving the Department of Insurance's post-disaster response, investing in wildfire prevention and increasing departmental transparency. He frames his approach as market reform rather than what he calls an untested large-scale public system.

polls.note: Names-only split sample. The other half of respondents, told that DSA endorses Kim and Allen is a 'mainstream Democrat', went Allen 36, Kim 23.

offices.likely_winner_basis: Two Democrats; Kim led the primary and both public polls narrowly, but 57-64% of voters were undecided and Allen holds the state party endorsement and heavier outside spending, so no clear favorite.
offices.summary: The first-ever Democrat-vs-Democrat general election for Insurance Commissioner pits former San Francisco Supervisor Jane Kim, endorsed by Bernie Sanders, the California Teachers Association and the Working Families Party, against state Sen. Ben Allen, endorsed by the California Democratic Party. Kim led the 11-candidate primary with 27.40% to Allen's 19.41%; the top Republican, Stacy Korsgaden, was eliminated at 15.54%. Kim proposes a state-run nonprofit natural-disaster insurance program, while Allen emphasizes using and strengthening the commissioner's existing regulatory powers (including his SB 1209, signed in September 2026).

incumbent.name: Tony Thurmond
incumbent.note: Term-limited; ran unsuccessfully for Governor (0.69% in primary).

offices.primary_note: Nonpartisan office elected by majority: no candidate reached 50% on June 2 (top finisher 22.64%), so the top two advance to a November runoff.

candidates.name: Sonja Shaw
candidates.bio: President of the Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education, elected in 2022; a Republican, she finished first in the June 2026 nonpartisan primary.
candidates.platform: Shaw's stated priorities are returning schools to fundamentals in reading, writing and math, citing that roughly half of California students are not at grade level; restricting girls' sports and bathroom access to biological females, which she frames as protecting girls under Title IX; and expanding parental involvement in education decisions. She also calls for reducing bureaucratic overhead and improving fiscal transparency so more resources reach classrooms.

candidates.name: Richard Barrera
candidates.bio: Member of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education since 2008, including as board president, and a senior policy adviser at the California Department of Education; a Democrat, he finished second in the June 2026 primary.
candidates.platform: Barrera emphasizes raising academic achievement, graduation rates and college and career readiness while narrowing achievement gaps, pointing to San Diego Unified's results as a model. He calls for building a sustainable teacher pipeline including affordable educator housing, securing school funding through bond measures, and modernizing aging school buildings. His voter-guide statement also prioritizes protecting students from federal immigration enforcement in schools, supporting LGBTQ+ students and maintaining vaccination requirements.

offices.likely_winner_basis: Barrera led the only public poll 26-20 with a majority undecided, holds the California Democratic Party and major education-labor endorsements, and the combined primary vote for Democratic-aligned candidates far exceeded Shaw's; a Republican-aligned candidate has not won this office since 1994.
offices.summary: Chino Valley school board president Sonja Shaw, a Republican known for the district's parental-notification policy on student gender identity, finished first in the 10-candidate nonpartisan primary (22.64%) and faces San Diego Unified board member Richard Barrera, a Democrat (20.30%), in a runoff. Democrats Nichelle Henderson, Al Muratsuchi, Anthony Rendon and Josh Newman split much of the remaining vote. Barrera has the state Democratic Party, CSEA and Equality California endorsements; the office is formally nonpartisan and party labels do not appear on the ballot.

incumbent.name: Ted Gaines
incumbent.note: Term-limited; running for El Dorado County Board of Supervisors.

candidates.name: Shannon Grove
candidates.bio: Republican state senator for District 12 (in the Senate since 2018, formerly Senate Republican Leader and a 2010-2016 Assemblymember), U.S. Army veteran and CEO of a Bakersfield staffing company she co-founded.
candidates.platform: Grove's voter-guide statement says she is running to protect the American Dream and lists defending Proposition 13, opposing what she calls excessive taxation on homes and businesses, and supporting economic growth as priorities. Her campaign site emphasizes the board's role in ensuring fairness and uniformity in county property-tax assessment and highlights her business and legislative background, with limited additional policy detail.

candidates.name: Nelson Esparza
candidates.bio: Democratic Fresno City Councilmember (District 7) first elected in 2018, an educator and economist raised in Madera; ballot designation Teacher/Economist/Councilmember.
candidates.platform: Esparza's voter-guide statement describes him as a champion for working families and small businesses, citing his work on the Fresno council's Finance and Audit Committee. He says he will work to close tax loopholes, oppose new taxes on middle- and working-class families, and ensure fair property-tax assessments. His campaign site lists education, healthcare, public safety and economic development as focus areas with limited further detail.

offices.likely_winner_basis: The primary was nearly tied (Grove 34.46%, Esparza 34.05%); the inland district is the only BOE seat held by a Republican (Gaines won 55.5% in 2022) and combined primary votes split roughly 51% R / 49% D, so it is a genuine toss-up with no polling.
offices.summary: Republican state Sen. Shannon Grove of Bakersfield, a former Senate GOP leader, and Democratic Fresno City Councilmember Nelson Esparza are competing for the open inland seat held by term-limited Republican Ted Gaines. Grove edged Esparza by about 8,000 votes in the five-candidate primary. District 1 stretches from the Oregon border through the Sacramento and San Joaquin valleys to most of San Bernardino County.

candidates.name: Sally Lieber
candidates.bio: Incumbent District 2 member and current chair of the Board of Equalization, elected in 2022, previously a State Assemblymember (2002-2008) and mayor of Mountain View.
candidates.platform: Lieber's campaign lists transparency and accountability (including a corporate-free campaign), fully staffing the board with trained personnel to help taxpayers, scrutiny of programs that fund affordable housing and transparent use of state tax credits, and services for veterans, homeowners, seniors, people with disabilities and small businesses. Her voter-guide statement highlights expanding access to property-tax relief and support for Proposition 13; she has defended keeping the board as a lean, effective forum for taxpayers.

candidates.name: John Pimentel
candidates.bio: San Mateo County Community College District trustee, former California Deputy Secretary for Transportation and clean-energy business executive.
candidates.platform: Pimentel's stated priorities are eliminating the sales tax on food (including restaurant, prepared and delivered food), closing corporate and high-wealth tax loopholes such as the water's-edge election and carried interest, and increasing transparency and accountability at the board. He also calls for modernizing property-tax administration with better data tools for county assessors and faster assessment appeals, and has said he would support folding the board's functions into other state tax agencies.

offices.likely_winner_basis: Lieber won an outright majority (56.76%) in the primary, more than 40 points ahead of fellow Democrat Pimentel (15.80%).
offices.summary: Incumbent Democrat Sally Lieber, a former Assemblymember elected to the board in 2022 with 69.8%, faces fellow Democrat John Pimentel, a San Mateo County Community College District trustee, after four Republicans split the remaining primary vote. District 2 covers the coast from Del Norte County through the Bay Area to Ventura County.

incumbent.name: Tony Vazquez
incumbent.note: Term-limited; ran unsuccessfully for State Treasurer (7.09% in primary).

candidates.name: Mike Gipson
candidates.bio: State Assemblymember for the 65th District since 2014 and chair of the Assembly Revenue and Taxation Committee; a former Carson City Councilmember, police officer and chief of staff to a former Board of Equalization chair.
candidates.platform: Gipson's campaign is framed around 'Fairness. Transparency. Accountability.' with stated goals of ensuring large corporations pay their fair share, protecting taxpayers and increasing transparency at the board. His voter-guide statement pledges to close tax loopholes used by wealthy insiders and powerful corporations so funding is available for health care, schools and other services; coverage also cites expanded outreach to homeowners and small businesses and prioritizing audits and oversight.

candidates.name: Samuel P. Sukaton
candidates.bio: Labor organizer (lead organizer for AFT Local 1521, the Los Angeles College Faculty Guild), former state advocacy coordinator for California Environmental Voters and former Inland Southern California director for the 2020 Bernie Sanders campaign.
candidates.platform: Sukaton's campaign lists four pillars: fair and uniform property assessments across counties with equal treatment for homeowners and small businesses; transparency and modernization of tax systems, including exploring split-roll reform; fiscal responsibility in managing revenues; and equitable growth that protects the environment. He also emphasizes stronger oversight of county assessors, expanded outreach about tax credits and exemptions for veterans, seniors and low-income homeowners, and streamlining the appeals process. He did not submit a voter-guide statement.

offices.likely_winner_basis: Gipson, a six-term Assemblymember, led the 10-candidate primary by nearly 10 points over labor organizer Sukaton; no polling.
offices.summary: Assemblymember Mike Gipson (D-Carson) and labor organizer Samuel Sukaton (D) advanced from a 10-candidate primary for the open Los Angeles County seat held by term-limited Democrat Tony Vazquez. Gipson took 27.88% to Sukaton's 18.21%, with former Monterey Park councilmember Yvonne Yiu (12.78%) and two Republicans eliminated. District 3 consists solely of Los Angeles County.

candidates.name: Denis Bilodeau
candidates.bio: Orange City Councilmember and Mayor Pro Tem, a director of the Orange County Water District since 2000, president of the Orange Taxpayers Association, and a licensed civil engineer with a Chapman University law degree.
candidates.platform: Bilodeau's stated priorities are protecting Proposition 13 and property rights, opposing new taxes, government accountability and exposing wasteful spending, closing special-interest tax loopholes, and supporting small business. His voter-guide statement says his goal is to lower the cost of living, pointing to utility assessments and his record of 'fighting for ratepayers'; he has signed the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association pledge.

candidates.name: Tom Umberg
candidates.bio: State Senator for District 34 since 2018 and chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee; a former Assemblymember, federal prosecutor, deputy drug czar under President Clinton and retired U.S. Army colonel.
candidates.platform: Umberg frames himself as an independent 'watchdog' and lists catching fraud, waste and abuse; fairness and consistency in applying tax rules to families and small businesses; ensuring large corporations and utilities are assessed accurately; refusing special-interest influence over assessments and supporting structural board reforms; consumer protection; and ensuring California claims federal dollars it is owed. His voter-guide statement emphasizes making 'big monied corporations pay their fair share.'

offices.likely_winner_basis: Bilodeau was the only Republican and led the primary with 45.06%, but the three Democrats combined for 53.4% and Schaefer (D) won the seat with 58.8% in 2022; with no polling the general is uncertain, leaning Democratic on district fundamentals.
offices.summary: Orange City Councilmember Denis Bilodeau (R) and state Sen. Tom Umberg (D-Santa Ana) are competing for the open Southern California seat held by term-limited Democrat Mike Schaefer. Bilodeau consolidated the Republican vote in the primary (45.06%) while Umberg (20.69%) narrowly beat Democrats Cody Petterson (18.39%) and Martin Arias (14.28%) for second. District 4 covers Orange, Riverside, San Diego and Imperial counties plus the San Bernardino Valley portion of San Bernardino County; the state Democratic Party endorsed Umberg after the primary.

boe_districts.note: San Bernardino County is split: most of the county (outside the San Bernardino Valley/panhandle) is in District 1.

San Bernardino County is split: the portion including Colton, Fontana, Grand Terrace, Highland, Loma Linda, Redlands, Rialto, San Bernardino, Twentynine Palms, Yucaipa and Yucca Valley is in District 4.

notes: Primary percentages are from the Secretary of State's certified Statement of Vote for the June 2, 2026 primary (as transcribed on Wikipedia).
Party codes: D Democratic, R Republican, NPP no party preference / nonpartisan office. The Superintendent race is nonpartisan; candidates' party registrations are given separately.

Ratings: Cook, Sabato and Inside Elections rate only the governor's race in 2026; Sabato's Crystal Ball issued one-time 2025 previews rating the AG and SoS races Safe D. Downballot ratings otherwise null.

props.title: Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs
props.summary: Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds: $10 billion for state housing programs (including about $7.2 billion for multifamily rental and supportive housing, $1.1 billion for homeownership and downpayment assistance, and smaller amounts for housing infrastructure, farmworker, student, tribal and local pilot housing) plus $1.25 billion for CalVet veterans' home loans. Placed on the ballot by the Legislature (SB 417, Limón). The LAO estimates the funds could subsidize up to 40,000 rental units and help up to 40,000 households buy homes.
props.yes_means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
props.no_means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
props.fiscal_impact: Increased state General Fund cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the $10 billion housing bond (about 0.25% of the General Fund budget); the $1.25 billion veterans' bond is repaid by veterans' loan payments at no direct state cost.
supporters: Senate President pro Tem Monique Limón
League of Women Voters of California
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO

props.title: Increases State's Rainy Day Fund
props.summary: Amends the Constitution to require deposits into the Budget Stabilization Account (rainy day fund) until it reaches 20% of General Fund tax revenues, up from the current 10% cap, with larger deposits in years when capital-gains revenues are unusually high. It extends required extra debt payments from 2030 to 2040 and broadens their allowed uses, and excludes reserve deposits from the state appropriations (Gann) limit until the money is withdrawn. Placed on the ballot by the Legislature (ACA 20, Gabriel).
props.yes_means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change; state budget reserves would be higher and the state would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
props.no_means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.
props.fiscal_impact: State budget reserves would be higher, because deposits would continue until the fund reaches 20% of General Fund taxes and more would be saved when revenues surge; the state might also make more debt payments by extending extra payments through 2040.
supporters: Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce
Linda Darling-Hammond, President, State Board of Education
Senate President pro Tem Monique Limón
League of Women Voters of California

props.title: Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes
props.summary: Makes permanent the higher personal income tax rates on high earners first approved by Proposition 30 (2012) and extended by Proposition 55 (2016), which are otherwise set to expire after 2030. The rates apply to income above roughly $371,000 for single filers, $742,000 for joint filers and $505,000 for heads of household (2025 levels, inflation-adjusted), paid by about the top 2% of taxpayers. Dedicated revenue is allocated 89% to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges, with administrative uses barred; the measure was placed on the ballot by petition, led by the California Teachers Association and California Federation of Teachers.
props.yes_means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
props.no_means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
props.fiscal_impact: Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue (varying with the stock market) by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent; roughly 40% of the money would go to schools and community colleges and the rest to other state programs and reserves.
supporters: California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO
League of Women Voters of California
opponents: Hispanic Chambers of Commerce of San Francisco

props.title: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns
props.summary: Proposition 4 (SB 42, Umberg; the 'California Fair Elections Act of 2026') repeals the 1988 Political Reform Act ban (enacted by Prop 73) on state and local governments using public funds for candidate campaigns, which currently applies to the state, counties, districts and general-law cities but not charter cities. It does not itself create any program; it allows governments to establish public campaign financing programs for candidates who agree to spending limits and meet eligibility criteria, bars using funds earmarked for education, transportation or public safety, bars using public funds for legal defense, fines or repaying personal loans, and triples the maximum fine for foreign-entity contributions.
props.yes_means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how they could be used, and who could receive them.
props.no_means: The state and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for candidates.
props.fiscal_impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs; costs of any future programs would depend on decisions by state and local governments.
supporters: League of Women Voters of California
California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO
opponents: California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce (president signed official argument against)

props.title: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers
props.summary: Proposition 5 (SCA 1, Newman) amends the state constitution so that recall elections for state officers ask only whether to remove the officer, eliminating the simultaneous election of a replacement. If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would serve for the rest of the term or until a successor is elected at a special election, depending on timing; other vacancies would be filled by special election or appointment under existing vacancy law, and a recalled officer could run in that special election.
props.yes_means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy; vacancies would instead be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
props.no_means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
props.fiscal_impact: Possible state and local government savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer recall elections, depending on the office recalled and how often recalls occur; these costs or savings would be rare.
supporters: League of Women Voters of California
California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
opponents: Sen. Brian W. Jones, Senate Minority Leader

props.title: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes
props.summary: Authorizes the California Housing Finance Agency to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund fixed-rate second-mortgage loans covering up to 17% of the purchase price of a newly built home sold for the first time, below county price caps. Borrowers must be California residents for at least a year, occupy the home, earn no more than 200% of area median income and put at least 3% down; bonds are repaid from borrowers' mortgage payments rather than state funds, and developers may opt into higher labor standards in exchange for modified construction-defect liability rules.
props.yes_means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program and could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund it.
props.no_means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
props.fiscal_impact: No direct state or local costs, because payments from homebuyers would repay bond investors; the program's scope and impact depend on unknown factors such as investor demand for the bonds and whether it increases home construction and buying.
supporters: Robert Hertzberg, former Senate Majority Leader (sponsor)
United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America
California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO

props.title: Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research
props.summary: Authorizes $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, with at least $4.2 billion for research on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease. Half the money goes to a single UC-affiliated nonprofit research institute selected by the Department of Public Health under criteria in the measure; the other half is distributed as competitive grants to public and nonprofit universities and institutes. Funding recipients must sell resulting drugs and technology in California at 20% below the national average price, and the General Fund receives 10% of licensing royalties until the bonds are repaid.
props.yes_means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
props.no_means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
props.fiscal_impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the bonds (roughly one-quarter of 1 percent of the General Fund budget). The state could recover part or all of this cost in later decades if the funded research generates revenue, but the amount and timing are uncertain.
supporters: Gary K. Michelson / Michelson Center for Public Policy (sponsor and principal funder)
The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research
opponents: Robert M. Kaplan, Ph.D., Stanford University School of Medicine (signed official argument against)
No on Proposition 38 (California Health Policy Strategies)
League of Women Voters of California
Orange County Register, San Diego Union-Tribune, Sacramento Bee and San Francisco Chronicle editorial boards

props.title: Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification
props.summary: Amends the state constitution to require voters to present government-issued identification to vote in person, and to provide a government-issued ID number on their registration and write its last four digits on their mail-ballot envelope. Requires the state to issue a free voter ID card on request, requires state and county officials to verify registered voters' citizenship using available government data and report county verification rates annually, and requires the State Auditor to audit compliance every odd-numbered year. California currently verifies voter identity by signature.
props.yes_means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
props.no_means: A voter's identity would continue to be established with the voter's signature.
props.fiscal_impact: State and local government costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements; costs depend on future decisions by the Legislature, state departments, local governments and voters.
supporters: Californians for Voter ID, Yes on 39 (campaign committee)
Bill Jones, former Secretary of State
Southern California News Group editorial boards
opponents: League of Women Voters of California
U.S. Sens. Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff
Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and Senate President pro Tem Monique Limon

props.title: Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers
props.summary: Imposes a one-time tax of 5% on the net worth of California residents whose covered assets exceed $1 billion, valued as of December 31, 2026 and payable in 2027 with an option to pay over five years. Covered assets include businesses, securities, art, collectibles and intellectual property but exclude real property and some pensions and retirement accounts. Allocates 90% of revenue to health care and 10% to food assistance or education programs, requires the money to supplement rather than replace existing funding, and exempts the revenue from the constitutional school-funding guarantee, budget-reserve and spending-limit rules.
props.yes_means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
props.no_means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
props.fiscal_impact: Temporary state revenue increase that probably would add up to tens of billions of dollars spread over several years, plus state administrative costs of up to tens of millions of dollars per year for several years. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue collected from billionaires.

props.title: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes
props.summary: Nullifies any state tax enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempts its revenues from the voter-approved 1979 state spending (Gann) limit. Requires the State Auditor to audit the programs that would receive funding before a voter-proposed statewide special tax goes on the ballot, with a summary printed in the voter guide, plus recurring audits of programs funded by special taxes enacted after January 1, 2026. Declares conflicting measures on the same ballot void if Prop 41 receives more votes, which is how it would neutralize Proposition 40.
props.yes_means: The State Auditor would review programs funded by voter-proposed special taxes before and after they appear on the ballot, and the state could not exclude new special-tax spending from its spending limit.
props.no_means: The State Auditor's responsibilities and the state spending limit requirements would not change.
props.fiscal_impact: Net fiscal effect unknown, depending on future decisions by voters and the Legislature. State Auditor costs would rise, likely in the low millions of dollars per year, mostly paid from new special-tax revenues; possible savings if audit recommendations are implemented.
supporters: Building a Better California (principal funder, backed largely by Sergey Brin)
San Diego Union-Tribune and Orange County Register editorial boards
opponents: League of Women Voters of California
Tax the Ultra-Rich Now, Yes on 3 & 40, No on 41 & 42 (committee)

props.title: Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes
props.summary: Amends the state constitution to prohibit any new state tax on the ownership of personal property (everything other than real estate, including business interests, intellectual property and financial assets such as retirement and investment accounts) and any new state tax that applies retroactively based on a taxpayer's prior conduct or status. Applies to taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026, and provides that conflicting measures on the same ballot are void if Prop 42 gets more votes, making it a direct counter-measure to Proposition 40.
props.yes_means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
props.no_means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
props.fiscal_impact: Possibility that state tax revenues will not go up as much in the future because the measure restricts the state's options for raising taxes; when and by how much is unclear.
supporters: State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
Peace Officers Research Association of California
Building a Better California (principal funder, backed largely by Sergey Brin)
San Diego Union-Tribune and Orange County Register editorial boards
opponents: Tax the Ultra-Rich Now, Yes on 3 & 40, No on 41 & 42 (committee)
Sacramento Bee and San Francisco Chronicle editorial boards

props.title: Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
props.summary: Raises the vote needed to approve voter-proposed (citizen-initiative) local special taxes from a simple majority to two-thirds beginning January 1, 2027, matching the Proposition 13 threshold that already applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local governing bodies, and bars local governments from imposing additional ad valorem real-property taxes except as the Constitution already allows. It responds to appellate rulings after the 2017 Upland decision that let initiative special taxes pass by majority vote. The Legislature placed it on the ballot (ACA 22, Wicks) as a compromise under which the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association withdrew a broader initiative.
props.yes_means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.
props.no_means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.
props.fiscal_impact: Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes; the actual revenue impact depends on future decisions by local governments and voters.
supporters: California Business Roundtable Issues PAC (lead funder)
San Diego Union-Tribune and Southern California News Group editorial boards
opponents: Non-Profit Housing Association of Northern California
Asm. Buffy Wicks (ACA 22 author, opposes the measure)

props.title: Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services
props.summary: Requires private nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics serving low-income and uninsured patients) to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on 'program services' advancing their charitable health care mission, limiting administrative and other spending to 10%. Clinics that fall short would pay a penalty to the state equal to the shortfall, refundable if they comply within five years; the Attorney General would define qualifying expenses and the state could grant temporary waivers.
props.yes_means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
props.no_means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
props.fiscal_impact: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year to enforce the new requirements, covered by fees charged to affected clinics. Other uncertain state and local costs depending on how expenses are defined and whether clinics comply or close.
opponents: American College of Emergency Physicians, California
National Association of Social Workers, California Chapter

props.title: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects
props.summary: Amends the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to create optional expedited review procedures for projects it defines as 'essential,' including most housing, transportation, water, health care, school, clean energy and wildfire-prevention projects. It sets binding deadlines for agencies to complete environmental review and permitting, narrows the alternatives analysis and other review requirements, and sets deadlines and limits on the scope of court challenges to project approvals.
props.yes_means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures with tighter time limits for environmental review and a reduced scope of what courts can consider.
props.no_means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
props.fiscal_impact: Initial costs for state and local governments likely in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually, partly covered by fees. In the longer term, uncertain but potentially more significant positive or negative fiscal effects depending on how many eligible projects get built and their environmental impacts.
opponents: League of Women Voters of California

candidates.bio: Democratic assemblymember since 2022 for eastern San Francisco; former San Francisco supervisor (2019-2022) and school board member; Stanford JD.
candidates.platform: Campaign site emphasizes building more housing near jobs and transit with renter protections, expanded homelessness interventions (supportive housing, mental health and addiction treatment), and addressing income inequality.

candidates.name: Manuel Noris-Barrera
candidates.bio: Realtor and 2024 runner-up in this district; qualified for the November ballot as a write-in with 468 primary votes (no ballot designation).

17.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent was the only name on the primary ballot and took 99.4%; his opponent advanced as a write-in with 0.4%.
17.summary: Democratic incumbent Matt Haney faces Republican write-in Manuel Noris-Barrera, who qualified with 468 votes, in a deep-blue San Francisco district.

candidates.name: Mia Bonta
candidates.bio: Democratic assemblymember since 2021 for Oakland, Alameda and Emeryville; chair of the Assembly Health Committee, former Oakland Promise nonprofit executive and Alameda school board president; Yale JD.
candidates.platform: Campaign site emphasizes defending Medi-Cal and health-care protections from federal cuts, community safety through prevention and accountability, housing affordability, and immigrant protection.

candidates.name: Andre Sandford
candidates.bio: Housing program director with degrees from Jacksonville State University; ran as the American Independent runner-up in this district in 2024.

18.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent took 76.9% of the primary against the same opponent, who received 10.9%.
18.summary: Two Democrats advanced; incumbent Mia Bonta faces Andre Sandford, her 2024 opponent, in one of the most Democratic districts in the state.

candidates.name: Catherine Stefani
candidates.bio: First-term Democratic assemblymember (elected 2024), attorney and former San Francisco supervisor for District 2 (2018-2024); affiliated with Moms Demand Action.
candidates.platform: Campaign messaging centers on making California 'safer and more affordable'.

candidates.name: Philip Wing
candidates.bio: Retired financial advisor (ballot designation 'Retired Financial Advisor').

19.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent took 83.0% of the two-candidate primary in a D+57 district.
19.summary: Democratic incumbent Catherine Stefani faces Republican Philip Wing in a deep-blue western San Francisco district.

candidates.name: Liz Ortega
candidates.bio: Democratic assemblymember since 2022 for the southern East Bay; former Alameda Labor Council executive secretary-treasurer and AFSCME Local 3299 political director.
candidates.platform: Campaign site lists affordable workforce and family housing, living-wage jobs, ending homelessness (including fentanyl/naloxone legislation), reproductive freedom and neighborhood and school safety.

candidates.name: Patricia Muga
candidates.bio: Real estate appraiser (ballot designation 'Real Estate Appraiser').
candidates.platform: Campaign site emphasizes public safety: opposing reduced penalties for violent or repeat offenders, fully funding local law enforcement, restoring prosecutorial tools, and mental health and addiction services.

20.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent took 75.1% of the two-candidate primary in a D+40 district and won 72.9% in 2024.
20.summary: Democratic incumbent Liz Ortega faces Republican Patricia Muga in a safely Democratic Hayward-San Leandro district.

candidates.name: Diane Papan
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember first elected in 2022; former mayor and city councilmember of San Mateo.
candidates.platform: Campaign priorities include year-round wildfire prevention, a state constitutional protection for reproductive freedom, and expanding recycled and reclaimed water use.

candidates.name: Jabra Muhawieh
candidates.bio: Millbrae business owner, enrolled agent/tax professional and real estate broker who runs his family's tax firm and a San Francisco grocery business.
candidates.platform: Says he wants government accountable to taxpayers and focused on results, and more opportunity for working families, homeowners and small businesses.

21.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Harris +50.6; registration Feb 2023: 55.8% D, 14.2% R, 24.6% NPP
21.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent took 78.7% in a two-candidate primary in a D+50 district.
21.summary: Incumbent Democrat Diane Papan seeks a third term against Republican businessman Jabra Muhawieh in a safely Democratic San Mateo County seat.

candidates.name: Juan Alanis
candidates.bio: Republican Assemblymember first elected in 2022 after 27 years with the Stanislaus County Sheriff's Office.
candidates.platform: Emphasizes public safety and school security legislation, bipartisan problem-solving (co-chair of the Legislative Problem Solvers Caucus), and Valley agriculture and water issues.

22.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Trump +7.5; registration Feb 2023: 49.5% D, 15.6% R, 31.0% NPP
22.likely_winner_basis: Only candidate on the ballot; unopposed in the primary and general.
22.summary: Incumbent Republican Juan Alanis is unopposed for a third term; he was the only candidate to file.

candidates.name: Marc Berman
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember since 2016, chair of the Business and Professions Committee; seeking his sixth and final term.
candidates.platform: Legislative focus on higher education policy, business and professional regulation, cybersecurity and electric-vehicle infrastructure.

candidates.name: David G. Johnson
candidates.bio: Chairman of the Santa Clara County Republican Party with 40 years in commercial construction, running two firms since 1994 and 2010.
candidates.platform: Opposes new taxes and regulations and supports parental rights and school choice.

23.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Harris +54.5; registration Feb 2023: 54.3% D, 14.5% R, 26.9% NPP
23.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent won 77.3% in the primary in one of the most Democratic districts in the state.
23.summary: Incumbent Democrat Marc Berman faces Santa Clara County GOP chair David G. Johnson, who edged out a second Republican in the primary; the seat is safely Democratic.

candidates.name: Alex Lee
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember first elected in 2020 representing San Jose, Milpitas, Fremont and Newark; seeking a fourth term.
candidates.platform: Priorities include affordable and social housing and reducing homelessness, expanding CalFresh and support for immigrant communities, and investing in schools and colleges.

candidates.name: Max Hsia
candidates.bio: Semi-retired businessman who owned a food and retail business in San Jose's Berryessa neighborhood and became active opposing regional sales-tax increases.
candidates.platform: Calls for reducing construction regulation to lower housing costs, expanding license-plate-reader technology and a low-level-crime task force, and merit-based teacher pay.

24.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Harris +30.6; registration Feb 2023: 49.7% D, 15.9% R, 30.1% NPP
24.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent took 65.4% in a three-way primary in a D+30 district.
24.summary: Incumbent Democrat Alex Lee faces Republican Max Hsia after an NPP Fremont councilmember was eliminated in the primary; the district is strongly Democratic.

candidates.name: Ash Kalra
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember since 2016 and former San Jose city councilmember, author of the California Racial Justice Act; seeking his sixth and final term.
candidates.platform: Priorities include renter and homeowner protections and homelessness policy, single-payer health care, and workplace protections and fair wages.

candidates.name: Himat Singh Bainiwal
candidates.bio: Attorney (ballot designation); little public campaign information available.

25.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Harris +32.4; registration Feb 2023: 52.5% D, 16.4% R, 25.8% NPP
25.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent won 72.2% in a two-candidate primary in a D+32 district.
25.summary: Incumbent Democrat Ash Kalra faces Republican attorney Himat Singh Bainiwal in a safely Democratic San Jose seat.

candidates.name: Patrick Ahrens
candidates.bio: First-term Democratic Assemblymember elected in 2024; former Foothill-De Anza Community College District trustee and legislative staffer.
candidates.platform: Committee work centers on aging and long-term care, health policy and biotechnology, and housing finance and child-care costs.

candidates.name: Tim Gorsulowsky
candidates.bio: Small business owner (ballot designation); no campaign website found.
candidates.platform: Has said he wants to change state law to give law enforcement and prosecutors more ability to charge offenders.

26.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Harris +45.3; registration Feb 2023: 51.5% D, 14.2% R, 30.4% NPP
26.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent took 75.4% in the primary in a D+45 district.
26.summary: First-term Democrat Patrick Ahrens seeks re-election against Republican small-business owner Tim Gorsulowsky in a safely Democratic Silicon Valley seat.

incumbent.name: Esmeralda Soria
incumbent.note: running for other office (State Senate District 14)

candidates.name: Brian Pacheco
candidates.bio: Fresno County Supervisor since 2015 and fourth-generation dairy farmer; former Kerman Unified school board president.
candidates.platform: Campaign emphasizes agriculture and water management, education, and senior and health-care services.

candidates.name: Mike Murphy
candidates.bio: Attorney and former mayor of Merced (2015-2020) who served on the Merced City Council from 2011.
candidates.platform: Pitches a bipartisan, cross-aisle approach to representing the Valley district in Sacramento.

27.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Trump +2.6; registration: 40% D, 29% R, 24% NPP; CalMatters rates the race Leans Democratic
27.likely_winner_basis: Slight lean only: Murphy led the primary 43.4-40.3, but Democrats combined for 56.6%, Pacheco holds a large cash advantage, and CalMatters rates it Leans Democratic; the district voted for Trump in 2024, so this is close to a toss-up.
27.summary: Open seat after Democrat Esmeralda Soria ran for State Senate. Republican former Merced mayor Mike Murphy topped the primary over Fresno County Supervisor Brian Pacheco (D) in a Latino-majority Valley district that voted for Trump in 2024; one of the most competitive Assembly races in the state.

candidates.name: Gail Pellerin
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember since 2022 and former Santa Cruz County Clerk; chairs the Assembly Elections Committee.
candidates.platform: Priorities include affordable housing and homelessness, affordable and equitable health care, and jobs and the economy.

candidates.name: Carol Pefley
candidates.bio: Real estate broker who founded a Silicon Valley brokerage in 2009 after a career in television news and radio.
candidates.platform: Focuses on reducing the cost of living and business regulation and opposing state-mandated housing upzoning in local communities.

28.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Harris +40.3; registration Feb 2023: 43.8% D, 19.4% R, 33.5% NPP
28.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent won 72.0% in a two-candidate primary in a D+40 district.
28.summary: Incumbent Democrat Gail Pellerin seeks a third term against Republican realtor Carol Pefley in a safely Democratic Santa Cruz/Santa Clara seat.

candidates.name: Robert Rivas
candidates.bio: Speaker of the California State Assembly, first elected in 2018; former two-term San Benito County Supervisor.
candidates.platform: Campaign themes are affordability, safe streets and housing.

candidates.name: Dennis Sanchez
candidates.bio: Central Coast small business owner and regional manager who trained with the Salinas Police Department and worked in construction and private security.
candidates.platform: Names public safety, affordability, housing and accountable government as priorities, with few detailed proposals published.

29.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Harris +44.0; registration Feb 2023: 50.8% D, 21.5% R, 21.2% NPP
29.likely_winner_basis: The Speaker took 66.5% in a three-way primary in a D+44 district.
29.summary: Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas seeks a fifth term against Republican small-business owner Dennis Sanchez, who narrowly beat 2024 runner-up J.W. Paine for the second spot; the seat is safely Democratic.

candidates.name: Dawn Addis
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember since 2022 and former special-education teacher and Morro Bay councilmember; chairs the Budget Subcommittee on Health.
candidates.platform: Priorities include fully funding public schools, expanding access to health care and protecting the environment.

candidates.name: Shannon Kessler
candidates.bio: Arroyo Grande business owner, former parks commissioner and PTA president, and founder of Save Girls' Sports Central Coast.
candidates.platform: Campaigns on public safety, housing affordability, government accountability and parental rights, including opposition to transgender athletes in girls' sports.

30.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent led the primary 54.8-35.9 and combined Democratic vote was 64% in a D+27 district.
30.summary: Incumbent Democrat Dawn Addis faces Republican Shannon Kessler, who has made girls' sports and parental rights central, in a Democratic-leaning Central Coast seat.

incumbent.name: Joaquin Arambula
incumbent.note: running for other office (Fresno City Council)

candidates.name: Annalisa Perea
candidates.bio: Fresno City Councilmember elected in 2022, certified city planner, and sister of former Assemblymember Henry T. Perea.
candidates.platform: Campaign emphasizes housing affordability, cost of living and support for working families.

candidates.name: Jim Polsgrove
candidates.bio: Fresno native and retired engineering technician with 39 years in civil service for the City and County of Fresno.
candidates.platform: Calls for tougher criminal laws, reducing state debt and lowering taxes, and protecting constitutional rights.

31.likely_winner_basis: Democrats combined for 65.6% of the primary vote in a D+13 Fresno district; Perea led with 44.6% and has a large fundraising edge.
31.summary: Open seat after Democrat Joaquin Arambula left to run for Fresno City Council. Fresno Councilmember Annalisa Perea (D) beat a rival in the primary and is favored over Republican retired engineer Jim Polsgrove.

candidates.name: David Couch
candidates.bio: Kern County Supervisor since 2013 and former Bakersfield City Councilmember (1999-2012); endorsed by retiring incumbent Stan Ellis.
candidates.platform: Lists affordability, crime and homelessness, water and energy policy, and support for oil, agriculture and small business as priorities.

32.summary: Open seat: Republican Stan Ellis, who won a 2025 special election, is not running, and Kern County Supervisor David Couch (R) is unopposed.

candidates.name: Alexandra Macedo
candidates.bio: First-term Republican Assemblymember from Tulare elected in 2024; became Assembly Republican Leader in August 2026.
candidates.platform: As GOP leader she has focused on California's affordability crisis and pushing back on Sacramento policies; committee work covers judiciary and consumer protection.

candidates.name: Hipolito Angel Cerros
candidates.bio: Former mayor and city councilmember of Lindsay, first-generation UC Davis graduate, and 2024 candidate for this seat.
candidates.platform: Emphasizes public safety and water infrastructure funding, and parks and street improvements.

33.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent and Assembly GOP leader won 61.2% in a two-candidate primary in an R+18 district.
33.summary: Republican Alexandra Macedo, now Assembly Republican Leader, faces a rematch-style challenge from Democrat Hipolito Cerros in a safely Republican Valley seat.

candidates.name: Charles Hughes
candidates.bio: Antelope Valley Union High School District trustee, retired law enforcement officer, Navy veteran and small business owner.
candidates.platform: Calls for cutting taxes and regulation including the gas tax, public safety and the fentanyl crisis, and vocational training and parental choice in education.

candidates.name: Randall Putz
candidates.bio: Mayor of Big Bear Lake and city councilmember since 2014, former Bear Valley Unified school board member; a former Republican now running as a Democrat.
candidates.platform: Emphasizes expanding rural health-care access in San Bernardino County, affordable housing and public education funding.

34.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Trump +19.8; registration Feb 2023: 27.7% D, 44.5% R, 22.6% NPP
34.likely_winner_basis: Putz led the primary as the lone Democrat, but Republicans combined for 60.8% in an R+20 district with a 17-point GOP registration edge.
34.summary: Open seat with Republican Tom Lackey termed out. Democrat Randall Putz topped a split primary, but Republican Charles Hughes is favored in November in this heavily Republican high-desert district.

incumbent.name: Jasmeet Bains
incumbent.note: running for other office (U.S. House, CA-22)

candidates.name: Andrae Gonzales
candidates.bio: Bakersfield City Councilmember since 2016 and Vice Mayor, executive director of the nonprofit Stewards, former school board trustee, and 2024 candidate for this seat.
candidates.platform: Priorities include improving schools and early education, lowering costs of gas, groceries and prescriptions, and expanding health care including a Kern County medical school.

candidates.name: Saul Ayon
candidates.bio: Mayor of McFarland, retired Kern County Sheriff's deputy with about 25 years in law enforcement, and high school criminal justice instructor.
candidates.platform: Campaigns on public safety, affordable living and clean water.

35.likely_winner_basis: Toss-up: Gonzales and Ayon finished 39 votes apart (18,338 to 18,299) in the primary; Democrats combined for 63% but the district split evenly in the 2024 presidential race.
35.summary: Open seat after Democrat Jasmeet Bains ran for Congress. Bakersfield Vice Mayor Andrae Gonzales (D) and McFarland Mayor Saul Ayon (R) were effectively tied in the primary in a Kern County district Harris carried by less than half a point.

candidates.name: Jeff Gonzalez
candidates.bio: First-term Republican Assemblymember who flipped the seat in 2024; 21-year Marine Corps combat veteran, former pastor and small business owner.
candidates.platform: Runs on affordability, public safety, improved education and bipartisan leadership, with emphasis on in-home supportive services for families caring for people with disabilities.

candidates.name: Ida Obeso-Martinez
candidates.bio: Mayor of Imperial and nurse practitioner with a Doctorate in Nursing Practice and more than 20 years in emergency, intensive and family care.
candidates.platform: Campaign centers on affordable health care, stronger schools, infrastructure and economic opportunity, and public safety through prevention and mental-health services.

36.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Trump +1.2; registration: 41% D, 29% R, 23% NPP; CalMatters rates the race Leans Democratic
36.likely_winner_basis: Toss-up: the Republican incumbent took 44.6% against three Democrats who combined for 55.4%, holds a large cash advantage, and the district narrowly voted for Trump in 2024, while CalMatters rates it Leans Democratic.
36.summary: Republican Jeff Gonzalez, who flipped this Coachella Valley/Imperial County seat in a 2024 upset, faces Imperial Mayor Ida Obeso-Martinez (D) in one of the state's marquee Assembly contests.

candidates.name: Gregg Hart
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember since 2022, former Santa Barbara County Supervisor and four-term Santa Barbara city councilmember.
candidates.platform: Priorities include equity and criminal justice reform, environmental protection and education.

candidates.name: Sari Domingues
candidates.bio: Santa Maria native and retired business analyst with a 30-year government career; 2024 runner-up for this seat.

37.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Harris +24.0; registration Feb 2023: 45.8% D, 25.3% R, 23.7% NPP
37.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent led the two-candidate primary 62.5-37.5 in a D+24 district and won the same matchup 60.7-39.3 in 2024.
37.summary: Rematch of 2024: incumbent Democrat Gregg Hart against Republican Sari Domingues in a Democratic-leaning Santa Barbara County seat.

candidates.name: Steve Bennett
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember since 2020, former 20-year Ventura County Supervisor and high school teacher; seeking a fourth term.
candidates.platform: Record emphasizes open-space protection (SOAR initiatives), campaign finance reform and fiscal discipline.

candidates.name: Michael MacDonald
candidates.bio: Ventura City Clerk since 2022, former Berkeley assistant city clerk and chair of the Oakland Public Ethics Commission.

38.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Harris +23.9; registration Feb 2023: 34.3% D, 33.4% R, 26.8% NPP
38.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent beat his fellow Democrat 69.4-30.6 in a two-candidate primary with no Republican on the ballot.
38.summary: Democrat-vs-Democrat general: incumbent Steve Bennett faces Ventura City Clerk Michael MacDonald after no Republican filed; Bennett is heavily favored.

candidates.name: Juan Carrillo
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember since 2022, former Palmdale city councilmember and city planner; chairs the Assembly Local Government Committee.
candidates.platform: Priorities include expanding affordable housing, small-business assistance programs and local-hire requirements on public works.

candidates.name: Paul Marsh
candidates.bio: U.S. Army veteran and mortgage-industry professional who serves on the Victorville Planning Commission and has run for office several times before.
candidates.platform: Emphasizes government accountability and responsible spending in Sacramento and financial relief for working families and small businesses.

39.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Harris +9.2; registration Feb 2023: 52.9% D, 15.1% R, 27.0% NPP
39.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent led the two-candidate primary 62.3-37.7 and the district has a large Democratic registration edge.
39.summary: Incumbent Democrat Juan Carrillo seeks a third term against Republican Paul Marsh in a Democratic-leaning Antelope Valley/Victorville district.

candidates.name: Pilar Schiavo
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember since 2022 representing the Santa Clarita Valley and northwest San Fernando Valley; chairs the Military and Veterans Affairs Committee.
candidates.platform: Legislative focus includes veterans affairs, electric-vehicle charging infrastructure, mental health and wildfire prevention.

candidates.name: Rickey Hayes II
candidates.bio: Marine Corps veteran, former law enforcement and custody officer, IBEW Local 47 lineman and energy-industry executive from the Santa Clarita Valley.
candidates.platform: Campaigns on public safety, rebuilding and modernizing the state's energy grid, and lowering the cost of living.

40.partisan_lean: 2024 presidential: Harris +8.4; registration Feb 2023: 42.3% D, 28.7% R, 22.2% NPP
40.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent took 55.6% against three Republicans who combined for 44.4% in a D+8 district she won 52.8-47.2 in 2024.
40.summary: Incumbent Democrat Pilar Schiavo faces Republican Rickey Hayes II, who emerged from a three-way GOP primary; the Santa Clarita-area seat leans Democratic but was competitive in 2024.

candidates.name: John Harabedian
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember for the 41st District since 2024, an attorney and former mayor and councilmember of Sierra Madre.
candidates.platform: His campaign site lists building affordable housing to reduce homelessness, combating climate change through renewable energy and water infrastructure, funding mental health treatment, investing in schools, gun-law enforcement, supporting local businesses and transit, and defending reproductive rights.

candidates.name: Adam Christopher Vena
candidates.bio: Monrovia sanitation worker and father; campaigns via social media.
candidates.platform: He says he entered the race over concerns about state overreach into family matters and overtaxation; he supports lowering taxes and gasoline costs, reducing regulation, faster wildfire recovery and brush clearance, and parental rights.

41.likely_winner_basis: First-term Democratic incumbent took 63.3% in the June primary in a district Harris carried by about 21 points; State Navigate rates it Solid D.
41.summary: Freshman Democrat John Harabedian (Pasadena/San Gabriel Valley foothills) faces Republican Adam Vena in a rematch of the two-candidate primary; not considered competitive.

incumbent.name: Jacqui Irwin
incumbent.note: termed out; running for U.S. House (CA-26)

candidates.name: Deborah Klein Lopez
candidates.bio: Agoura Hills city councilmember since 2018 and former mayor pro tem who previously worked as a State Senate and Assembly staffer and in financial analysis and project management; she chaired the Clean Power Alliance board from 2024 to 2026.
candidates.platform: Her campaign says she will focus on wildfire and disaster preparedness, lowering housing, healthcare, childcare, utility and home-insurance costs, expanding attainable housing, public safety, homelessness, education and environmental sustainability.

candidates.name: Ted Nordblum
candidates.bio: Republican small business owner from Thousand Oaks who built a medical device company over roughly 20 years after earlier work as a union heavy equipment operator; he was the 2024 runner-up in this district.
candidates.platform: His site's key issues are restoring affordability (cutting the gas tax, defending Prop 13, curbing spending), safe neighborhoods (more resources for law enforcement, tackling the fentanyl crisis), and protecting communities from wildfire threats and rising insurance costs.

42.likely_winner_basis: Lopez took 52.7% in the primary against two Republicans who split 47.3%; the district leans Democratic by double digits and State Navigate rates it Solid D (99.5%).
42.summary: Open seat (Ventura County / Conejo Valley) vacated by term-limited Democrat Jacqui Irwin. Agoura Hills councilmember Deborah Klein Lopez (D) faces repeat Republican nominee Ted Nordblum; the combined GOP primary vote (47.3%) makes this a Democratic-held seat that drew a serious challenge, but it still leans D.

candidates.name: Celeste Rodriguez
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember for the 43rd District since 2024 and former mayor and councilmember of San Fernando, with a USC master's in social work and 15-plus years running community programs.
candidates.platform: Her campaign lists economic opportunity, education and safe learning environments, environmental equity, family stability including maternal health and childcare, and homelessness and affordable housing, with an emphasis on protecting immigrant families.

candidates.name: Ricardo Benitez
candidates.bio: Republican plumber and electrical contractor and repeat candidate; no campaign website found.

43.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent took 74.9% in the two-candidate primary in a heavily Democratic San Fernando Valley district; State Navigate rates it Solid D.
43.summary: First-term Democrat Celeste Rodriguez (San Fernando / northeast Valley) faces repeat Republican candidate Ricardo Benitez; not competitive.

candidates.name: Nicholas "Nick" Schultz
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember for the 44th District since 2024 and chair of the Assembly Public Safety Committee, a former California deputy attorney general and former Burbank mayor and councilmember.
candidates.platform: His campaign site lists housing (easing construction and helping renters and first-time buyers), fully funding public schools, stopping rising costs of food, gas, utilities and healthcare, creating jobs including in entertainment, environmental protection, and crime prevention.

candidates.name: Carolyn Daniels
candidates.bio: Republican independent contractor and mother, a former Miss America who founded Safe Places for Abused Women and Children in 1992 and has lived in the district for 20 years.
candidates.platform: Her campaign argues Sacramento's supermajority has made California unaffordable and that 'housing first' has failed; she supports Prop 36 enforcement, backing police and crime victims, prioritizing mental health treatment, enforcing anti-camping laws, and lowering housing, gas and insurance costs.

44.likely_winner_basis: Incumbent won 71.2% in the primary against two Republicans combined at 28.8%; State Navigate rates it Solid D.
44.summary: First-term Democrat Nick Schultz (Burbank/Glendale area) faces Republican Carolyn Daniels, who edged out a second Republican for the runoff spot; not competitive.

candidates.name: James C. Ramos
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember for the 45th District since 2018, the first California Native American elected to the Legislature, and a former San Bernardino County supervisor from the San Manuel Indian Reservation.
candidates.platform: His campaign site says his focus is helping the Inland Empire, highlighting resources for firefighters, being a strong voice for victims of crime, and support for law enforcement and union labor.

candidates.name: Greg Abdouch
candidates.bio: Republican small business owner and lifelong Inland Empire resident with roughly 30 years in sales and entrepreneurship, including running a construction company.
candidates.platform: His campaign runs on 'Restoring Common Sense,' pledging to lower costs for housing, gas and everyday essentials through lower taxes and less regulation, restore public safety with stronger support for law enforcement (he backs Prop 36), and improve education.

45.likely_winner_basis: Four-term incumbent took 65.6% in the two-candidate primary; State Navigate rates the San Bernardino-area seat Solid D.
45.summary: Democrat James Ramos, seeking a fifth term, faces Republican small-business owner Greg Abdouch in a rematch of the primary; not competitive.

candidates.name: Jesse Gabriel
candidates.bio: Democratic Assemblymember for the 46th District since 2018 who chairs the Assembly Budget Committee and the Legislative Jewish Caucus; a Harvard Law graduate and former practicing attorney.

candidates.name: Tracey Schroeder
